title: Polar Bears Aren't White (0 White Hairs) 🐻‍❄️
description:
Why do polar bears have black skin under white fur? Polar bear hairs are clear and hollow with no white pigment, and they only look white because light scatters inside them, while most warmth comes from thick fat and fur that traps heat so well polar bears almost vanish on heat cameras.

topic: Why do polar bears have black skin under white fur?
script: If you shaved a polar bear, you'd find black skin. And zero white hairs. Why? Each hair is clear, like a tiny plastic straw with a hollow core full of air. There's no white pigment in it. So why does it look white? Light bounces around inside those clear hairs and scatters in every direction, the same trick that makes snow look white. Scientists once thought the hairs piped sunlight down to the skin like fiber optics. Turns out they don't. Most sunlight never reaches the skin. The black skin may soak up what little warmth gets through, but the real heater is underneath: up to eleven centimeters of fat, plus fur that traps heat so well polar bears almost vanish on heat cameras. So is a polar bear white, black, or totally see-through?
key_facts: Polar bears have black skin under their fur (Alaska Science Forum, SeaWorld)
Each hair is translucent with a hollow core and has no white pigment; it looks white because it scatters light (Alaska Science Forum)
The idea that hairs pipe sunlight to the skin like fiber optics was tested and found false; little sunlight reaches the skin (Alaska Science Forum, Live Science)
Blubber up to about 11 cm (4.5 in) thick (SeaWorld)
Polar bears lose so little heat they are nearly invisible to infrared cameras (Live Science)
